row.title: Eupompus Gave Splendour to Art of Numbers
row.author: Aldous Huxley

plot_extraction.response_text:
A narrator visits his brilliant, eccentric friend Emberlin, who announces that he has solved an obscure literary mystery: Ben Jonson’s remark that “Eupompus gave splendour to Art by Numbers.” Drawing on a rare scholarly work, Emberlin recounts how Eupompus, a successful Alexandrian portrait painter, abandoned conventional art after becoming obsessed with counting and convinced that numbers were the only certain reality.

Eupompus began painting enormous, meticulously enumerated scenes, including thirty-three thousand black swans and crowds arranged in mathematical patterns. His admirers, the Philarithmics, treated counting as contemplation. His art grew increasingly abstract as he tried to depict ideas, pure number, and ultimately the totality of God and the universe. Before completing his final work, he killed two disciples with a hammer and then leapt to his death.

Four months after telling this story, Emberlin has himself become a devoted Philarithmic. He compulsively counts tiles, footsteps, distances, and other trivial quantities, while every conversation turns to numerical facts and speculations. His friends’ warnings fail, and his formerly rich intellect deteriorates into a narrow obsession. The narrator concludes that Eupompus may have killed himself not because he had finally gone mad, but because a sudden return of sanity revealed the absurdity and degradation into which his numerical fanaticism had led him.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story adopts the manner of an erudite intellectual satire, combining the club-room anecdote, the mock-scholarly essay and the fantastic cautionary tale. It is narrated retrospectively in the first person by an educated, socially assured observer whose chief function is to introduce and interpret the more eccentric Emberlin. The narrator is not neutral: he is amused, indulgent, cultivated and increasingly appalled. His frequent qualifications—“I confess,” “I rather believe,” “I have no doubt”—create the impression of spontaneous personal recollection while also allowing irony to operate at a slight distance. He initially admires Emberlin’s verbal magic and accommodates his childish vanity, but the closing passages replace affectionate mockery with disgust and moral alarm.

The prose is ornate, allusive and self-consciously literary. Its diction blends conversational English with Latinate abstractions, archaic turns and specialist vocabulary: “post-prandial,” “thaumaturge,” “unencyclopædic,” “Fons Deitatis,” “quincunxes” and “philarithmic.” References to Mallarmé, Meredith, Ben Jonson, Petronius, Giordano Bruno, Raymond Lully and Neoplatonism construct a dense atmosphere of cultivated learning. This erudition is both genuine and comic. Scholarship becomes a field of social play, obscure names are treated as common knowledge, and invented or marginal authorities are presented with solemn confidence. The exchange concerning “not the familiar Zuylerius” is characteristic: the narrator’s flippant assent is mistaken for learned agreement, exposing Emberlin’s pedantry without directly puncturing it.

Sentences are often long, balanced and elaborately subordinated. Parentheses, dashes, semicolons and qualifying clauses reproduce the rhythms of polished conversation and discursive thought. The narrator readily digresses from the immediate story into character portraiture, aesthetic reflection and comic speculation, then draws attention to the digression with phrases such as “But let that pass; I am straying from my purpose.” Such self-corrections make the prose seem leisurely and improvisatory while keeping it carefully controlled. Periodic constructions and rhetorical parallelism lend weight to absurd claims: counting is elevated into metaphysics, and an eccentric artistic movement is described in the language of philosophical history. Shorter sentences are reserved for comic emphasis or narrative turns, as when Emberlin’s fate is summarized starkly after the long embedded account.

Dialogue is highly stylized rather than naturalistic. Emberlin’s speech is fluent, expansive and lecture-like, filled with parenthetical distinctions, bibliographical explanations and speculative reconstruction. The narrator’s shorter questions and ironic prompts serve as cues for Emberlin’s monologues. Repetition supplies several comic motifs, especially “A discovery about Discoveries” and “Eupompus gave splendour to Art by Numbers.” The repeated sentence changes from an intriguing scholarly puzzle into an anthem, an obsession and finally the formula of a destructive creed. Verbal comedy also comes from disproportion: trivial information is treated with metaphysical solemnity, while madness and murder are discussed as unfortunate complications in an aesthetic history.

The structure is framed and recursive. It begins with Emberlin announcing his discovery, pauses for an extended portrait of him, returns to the conversation, and then contains a second story—the history of Eupompus—within Emberlin’s account. After that inset narrative reaches its grotesque conclusion, the frame advances four months and reveals that Emberlin has begun to repeat Eupompus’s pathology. The historical anecdote therefore functions as both exposition and prophecy. This architecture gives the story the shape of a mock case study: an obscure textual phrase produces research, research uncovers a forgotten doctrine, and the doctrine infects its discoverer. The compressed final section converts speculative comedy into a narrative of mental deterioration.

The pacing is deliberately uneven. The opening lingers over Emberlin’s personality, rooms, conversation and unpublished poetry, establishing a world in which ideas are more vivid than ordinary life. The central section slows further for detailed descriptions of imaginary paintings: thirty-three thousand black swans, geometrically arranged orchards, constellation-like crowds and a Cyclopean amphitheatre. These catalogues mimic antiquarian documentation while generating surreal visual force. The conclusion accelerates through examples of Emberlin’s new compulsions—counting tiles, steps and bodily rates—so that the grand metaphysics of Number collapses into repetitive, banal behaviour.

Tonally, the story moves from urbane amusement through whimsical fantasy to grotesque unease and finally caustic denunciation. Early images idealize intellectual conversation as intoxication, magic and a “crystal Eden.” Later images describe obsession as “mental leprosy” and reduce its sufferers to beasts, children and idiots. The narrator’s severity is itself darkly comic, particularly in his retrospective defence of Eupompus’s suicide and murders as a sane revolt against Eupompianism. This closing reversal depends on paradox: madness is presented as complacent system-building, while the flash of sanity manifests itself through violence and self-destruction.

A central stylistic device is mock elevation. Counting, one of the simplest mechanical operations, is transformed into an aesthetic and theological principle. The invented movement acquires a founder, disciples, terminology, masterpieces and a philosophy of reality. Capitalization—“Discoveries,” “Number,” “Pure Number,” “Art”—parodies the language by which abstractions are endowed with authority. Conversely, lofty speculation is repeatedly deflated by bath-time chanting, bathroom tiles, fingernail statistics and public lavatories. The oscillation between metaphysical grandeur and physical triviality generates much of the humour.

The imagery opposes two kinds of order. Emberlin’s early conversation creates a lucid, harmonious universe of ideas above the “hotch-potch” of ordinary existence; Eupompianism turns that desire for order into sterile enumeration. The imaginary paintings embody this corruption visually: identical forms, rigid groupings and numerical progressions replace human variety. Especially powerful is the amphitheatre in which thousands of one-eyed figures scrutinize the lone two-eyed creature. Its symmetry is menacing rather than beautiful, suggesting conformity, abstraction and collective fanaticism. The repeated emphasis on hard edges, planes, rows and exact quantities reinforces a movement from living complexity toward mechanical system.

The story’s humour is dry, hyperbolic and deadpan. Absurdities are not announced as jokes but embedded in precise, authoritative prose. Eupompus’s enormous fees, the reconstructed artistic movement and the elder Zuylerius’s “Dutch Latin” are narrated with pseudo-historical exactitude. Understatement sharpens the grotesquer moments: the murder of two disciples is folded into a summary of an unfinished artwork, and Eupompus’s splendour is described as “regrettably transient.” The narrator’s cultivated prejudices also contribute to the comic voice; his horror is directed less at danger than at boredom, vulgarity, bad conversation and the degradation of intelligence.

The thematic style is anti-systematic despite its scholarly surface. It distrusts ideas that claim to reduce experience to a single principle, particularly when aesthetic, religious and intellectual values are subordinated to quantification. It also satirizes the scholar’s susceptibility to the objects of his study: Emberlin does not merely interpret doctrines but compulsively reenacts them. Art, language and learning appear powerful enough to create alternative worlds, yet that power is morally ambiguous. Verbal imagination can liberate the mind from quotidian dullness, but an abstract formula can also colonize it. The result is a polished, densely allusive and fantastically comic style in which intellectual play gradually reveals the pathology concealed inside the desire for perfect order.

### THE SPLENDOUR OF EUPOMPUS

It was Emberlin who first explained to me the meaning of that cryptic sentence in Ben Jonson’s *Discoveries*: “Eupompus gave splendour to Art by Numbers.”

I had often read the sentence, and had as often allowed it to pass into that hospitable lumber-room of the memory where an educated man keeps quotations which he cannot explain but may someday have occasion to repeat. Jonson’s prose is full of such adamantine fragments. They have the air of inscriptions surviving from temples whose gods, rites and even architectural principles are forgotten; and I confess that I had never felt more curiosity concerning Eupompus than concerning the cook of Petronius or the more conscientious of the Neoplatonists.

Emberlin, however, was incapable of leaving a mystery alone. He telephoned to me one wet November afternoon and said, without preliminary civility:

“I have made a discovery about *Discoveries*.”

He paused, plainly expecting thunder.

“Not the authorship?” I asked.

“The authorship! My dear fellow, do not be Meredithian. No—the passage on Eupompus.”

“Of course.”

“You remember it?”

“Perfectly.”

“What does it mean?”

I told him that I had always supposed it meant what it said.

“That,” he replied, “is the last refuge of the unencyclopædic. Come at six.”

Emberlin inhabited three rooms above a maker of ecclesiastical vestments in Bloomsbury. The situation suited him. Through his windows one saw, according to the hour, either a grey wall, a yellow moon, or the upper half of an angel in a shop-sign; below, copes and chasubles slept in violet tissue-paper, while above them Emberlin constructed those aerial systems which were his chief luxury and, I rather believe, his only regular exercise.

His drawing-room was too crowded with books to appear untidy, for disorder ceases to offend when it becomes absolute. On the mantelpiece stood a bronze hand, a cracked astrolabe, two Chinese monsters, and a photograph of Mallarmé which Emberlin had framed upside down because, he said, it improved the forehead. Manuscripts occupied the chairs. The piano had not been opened for eleven years, though Emberlin was perpetually composing an opera upon Raymond Lully. Its libretto, he assured me, was complete except for the words.

He was at that time forty-two, though his face, which had preserved the innocence of a child and acquired the complexion of a bad winter, made any estimate hazardous. His eyes were bright, mobile and almost indecently intelligent. His conversation did not illuminate a subject so much as abolish the surrounding darkness. To pass an evening with him was to see the common universe—that hotch-potch of bills, pavements, appetites and parliamentary intelligence—dissolve, while in its place arose a crystal Eden of correspondences, analogies and delicious impossibilities. He could connect Giordano Bruno with the etiquette of umbrellas, or deduce from a spoon the melancholy of the late Roman Empire. That his conclusions were frequently false seemed a criticism of fact rather than of Emberlin.

He had, besides, the vanity proper to those who delight rather than succeed. Praise embarrassed him if it was general, but he accepted the minutest admiration with the gravity of a monarch receiving tribute. I had learned to humour him. When he showed me a poem of four lines, written in three alphabets and entitled *The Bronze Syllable*, I praised the caesura. There was no caesura, but the compliment nourished him for a week.

On the evening in question I found him seated before the fire, with a huge folio supported on his knees and a decanter at his elbow.

“You are late,” he said.

“By three minutes.”

“Two minutes and forty-seven seconds.”

I did not then observe the precision.

He poured me sherry and tapped the folio.

“This,” he said, “is Gaspard van Zuyler’s *De Artibus Numeralibus apud Alexandrinos*, Leyden, 1663.”

“Not the familiar Zuylerius?”

For a moment he looked almost offended.

“The elder Zuylerius, naturally. The familiar Zuylerius was his nephew and wrote on symbolic falconry. This is infinitely rarer. The British Museum copy disappeared in 1891, perhaps from shame. I found this in the library of Sir Andrew Pell, between a veterinary manual and the sermons of an uncle.”

“And he explains Eupompus?”

“He does not explain him. He reveals him. There is a difference.”

Emberlin leaned forward. The fire threw his large shadow over the books; and presently, in that room scented with dust, sherry and the ecclesiastical dyes from below, he began the history of Eupompus.

The man whom Jonson names so casually was, according to Zuylerius, an Alexandrian painter of the second century after Christ—not, Emberlin warned me, the earlier Eupompus of Sicyon, with whom he has been confused by scholars who deserve confusion. He enjoyed in youth a prodigious reputation as a portraitist. Governors, merchants, rhetoricians, courtesans and successful poisoners sat to him. He was especially admired for hands. One celebrated portrait represented the financier Cassianus counting gold; the fingers were so cunningly painted that three slaves, successively accused of stealing one of the coins, were tortured before the optical deception was discovered.

Eupompus received enormous fees, maintained a villa near Canopus, and might have died respectable had he not, at the age of thirty-nine, begun to count.

“The origin of the habit,” said Emberlin, “is disputed. Zuylerius attributes it to an afternoon spent waiting in the Baths of Hadrian. Cassiodorus Niger—whose authority is dubious but piquant—says that Eupompus counted the eyelashes of a dancing-girl and found the number prime. Personally, I accept the mosaic hypothesis.”

“What is that?”

“He observed that the floor of his studio contained twelve thousand nine hundred and sixty tiles.”

“Did it?”

“Almost certainly not. But the discovery, whether accurate or imaginary, transformed him.”

At first Eupompus merely introduced numerical exactitude into his pictures. If he painted a banquet, there were precisely forty guests, eighty sandals, two hundred fingernails and one hundred and seventeen olives. A hunting scene contained nine dogs, three boars, twenty-seven spears and three hundred and sixty-five trees, one for every day of the Egyptian year. His patrons were delighted. The enumeration of objects lent an agreeable solidity to ownership; a rich man, Emberlin remarked, likes to know not only that he possesses abundance but exactly how much abundance he possesses.

Soon, however, Eupompus became contemptuous of portraiture. The individual face seemed to him vague, accidental and morally disreputable. A nose could be long or short; a mouth might smile today and decay tomorrow; but Seven remained Seven even if Alexandria burned and the gods went bankrupt.

He began his first great philarithmic canvas, *The Black Swans*.

“It measured,” said Emberlin, consulting the folio, “ninety cubits by twenty-one.”

“Where did he hang it?”

“He did not hang it. He built a wall for it.”

Upon this Cyclopean surface Eupompus painted thirty-three thousand black swans advancing across a silver lake. They were arranged in eleven divisions of three thousand, each division subdivided into flocks of three hundred, thirty and three. No two birds occupied precisely the same attitude, though all possessed the same dimensions. In the foreground eleven dead swans floated upon their backs, their feet raised like black arithmetic signs against the water. The work required seven years and consumed so much lamp-black that the Alexandrian undertakers petitioned the prefect.

“What did it mean?” I asked.

Emberlin smiled pityingly.

“My dear fellow, it meant thirty-three thousand.”

The picture caused a sensation. Pilgrims came to count the swans, though no two pilgrims reached the same total. The more devout began again. One senator spent eighteen months before the canvas and died at the twenty-ninth thousand, whereupon his heirs accused Eupompus of concealing additional birds. The painter refused to defend himself, merely observing that error is personal but Number divine.

His disciples called themselves the Philarithmics—Lovers of Number. They maintained that counting was the purest form of contemplation because it alone permitted the mind to touch reality without soiling it by emotion. Beauty, courage, love and justice were, they said, regional superstitions; but four apples remained four even if the apples were sour, stolen, painted or theological. Their daily exercises included counting pebbles, breaths, roof-tiles, syllables, raindrops and the visible teeth of strangers. The advanced student was expected to count simultaneously in opposite directions.

Eupompus next painted *The Orchard of Proclus*. It represented one thousand and twenty-four trees arranged in quincunxes, each bearing a number of fruits corresponding to its distance from the central fountain. The fountain itself had sixteen basins, from which sixty-four streams descended by two hundred and fifty-six channels into a square pool. There were no people in the orchard. Humanity, Eupompus explained, would have ruined the progression.

After the orchard came *The Citizens under the Stars*: eight thousand four hundred persons standing in groups which reproduced the principal constellations. The rich formed Orion; slaves composed the Dragon; philosophers, being few and mutually hostile, were used for the smaller stars of the Lyre. Every citizen was painted with his mouth open, as if uttering his own number. From a distance the multitude resembled a yellowish cloud. From near at hand it was intolerable.

By then Eupompus had ceased to sell his works. Indeed, it was difficult to find buyers with adequate walls. He abandoned his villa and lived in an immense warehouse, sleeping beside a counting-board. His beard reached his girdle; his nails grew curved and translucent; and he ate beans, not from ascetic conviction, but because they were convenient to enumerate.

His doctrines also enlarged. Number, which had begun as a discipline of art, became the substance of the cosmos. The visible world was merely Number wearing a coloured cloak. Matter was interrupted arithmetic. Time was the counting of change; space, the counting of intervals; music, the counting of vibrations; virtue, the proper addition of acts. Even the gods were compelled to submit. Isis was Two because she was mother and widow; Serapis was Nine for reasons now unhappily lost; the supreme God was Zero and Infinity together—an identification which disturbed certain priests but delighted the tax-collectors.

“Neoplatonism?” I suggested.

“Neoplatonism is a fog through which one sometimes sees the moon. Eupompianism was an account-book in which the moon had been entered twice.”

His later paintings grew less representational and more alarming. One consisted solely of red squares diminishing toward a white centre. Another displayed six million blue points on a field of ochre. In *The Migration of the Units*, ten thousand naked figures walked from left to right, gradually losing their human features until the last was a perpendicular stroke. The work was praised by an elderly grammarian as the final conquest of accident.

There was also the amphitheatre.

Here Emberlin lowered his voice, though only the photograph of Mallarmé could have overheard us.

The picture showed a circular arena containing ninety-nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine Cyclopes. They occupied ascending tiers, one above another, each creature naked, hairless and provided with a single enormous eye. All those eyes were fixed upon the solitary figure in the arena: a small, ordinary man with two eyes. He stood with his arms hanging helplessly, conscious that his superfluous organ made him monstrous. The Cyclopes neither threatened nor applauded. They merely counted him.

I confess that the conception troubled me. There are absurdities which, if pursued with sufficient logic, become nightmares; and the lonely biped under that arithmetic scrutiny seemed to express something in modern existence which I had no wish to understand.

“Was that his masterpiece?” I asked.

“No. His masterpiece was never completed.”

In his sixty-third year Eupompus announced *The Totality*. This was to contain every possible object, event, relation, thought and number: the universe displayed not as chaos, but as an exact inventory. He ordered a circular building three hundred cubits in diameter. At its centre he prepared a panel of polished ivory representing the Fons Deitatis, from which concentric rings would proceed through Pure Number, intelligible form, celestial mechanism, animal life, human history, private memory and the uncounted dust of futurity.

“How does one paint every possible event?”

“With difficulty,” said Emberlin.

Eupompus worked for fourteen years. He completed Zero, Unity, the first nine primes, two-thirds of Geometry, five planets, the concept of thirst, all red insects, and the left side of Cleopatra. He had begun Remorse when the catastrophe occurred.

One morning two of his most faithful disciples, Ptolemon and Bion, found him counting the blows of a hammer upon the floor. Whether they interrupted, contradicted his total, or offered to assist is not known. Eupompus killed both of them with the hammer—Ptolemon with seven blows, Bion with nine—then climbed the unfinished dome and threw himself into the court below.

Thus, Emberlin concluded, the splendour which Eupompus gave to Art by Numbers was regrettably transient. His followers dispersed. The warehouse burned; the great canvases perished; the word “Philarithmic” survived only in three corrupt manuscripts and one abusive marginal note. Ben Jonson, who had encountered some late epitome of Zuylerius’s lost Greek source, preserved the sentence without comprehending its magnitude.

“And that,” Emberlin said, closing the folio, “is my discovery about *Discoveries*.”

The room had grown dark. On the table stood two glasses, the decanter, and a small heap of walnut shells which Emberlin had arranged in rows while speaking.

“It is a remarkable history,” I said. “Do you believe it?”

He stared at me.

“Belief is a vulgar relation between the mind and fact. I have demonstrated it.”

“But why did Eupompus kill himself?”

“Madness, obviously.”

“And the disciples?”

“A regrettable complication.”

We dined afterward at a little restaurant in Soho, where Emberlin embarrassed the waiter by asking how many peas accompanied the sole. He explained that he wished merely to test Zuylerius’s assertion that modern Europeans had lost the instinct of quantity. I thought nothing of it. Emberlin’s curiosity had always been omnivorous, and if he chose to digest his fish numerically, it was no concern of mine.

Four months later he was a Philarithmic.

The transformation did not announce itself dramatically. There were no black swans, no warehouse, no murders. He simply began to count everything.

He knew that there were eighty-six paving-stones between his door and the corner, one hundred and forty-two from the corner to the tobacconist’s, and six hundred and eleven from the tobacconist’s to the British Museum—unless he crossed obliquely, in which case the number was reduced by nineteen. He had calculated the average footsteps required to traverse Russell Square in rain, sunshine and intellectual agitation. He informed me that the staircase to his rooms contained forty-seven steps, though one was “metaphysically ambiguous” because of a landing.

His bathroom tiles numbered two thousand three hundred and four. He had counted them so often that he could chant their arrangement while bathing. His bedroom possessed seven hundred and ninety-one visible objects if dust-particles were excluded, and an indefinite but approachable number if they were not. He measured the growth of his fingernails, the oscillations of the gas-flame, the beats of his heart before and after coffee, and the hairs remaining upon his head. The last inquiry, being repeated nightly, depressed him but did not cure him.

Conversation became impossible. If one mentioned Shakespeare, Emberlin replied that the plays contained a certain number of commas. The Alps suggested cubic mileage; love, the pulse-rate; death, the probable sum of human corpses. When I praised a sunset, he estimated the angle occupied by the red cloud. When Mrs. Pelham announced her engagement, he asked how many letters had passed between the lovers. She answered, with some spirit, that there were things which could not be counted. Emberlin looked at her with infinite compassion.

His old learning did not disappear at once. It contracted. That splendid intellect, formerly a palace with windows opening upon every century, became a narrow corridor lined with numbered doors. Mallarmé, Bruno, Lully and Petronius were still admitted, but only after submitting their statistics. Poetry was “syllabic distribution”; painting, “enumerated pigment”; music, “audible proportion.” He abandoned his opera because the chorus refused, in imagination, to consist of exactly two hundred and fifty-six voices.

We remonstrated. Ferris appealed to his humour; Dr. Latham to medicine; I, less wisely, to pride. He defeated us all by counting our arguments. Mine, he said, contained twelve propositions, of which seven were repetitions, three sentimental, one insolent and one unverified.

Once, in desperation, I demanded whether he had reflected upon the end of Eupompus.

“Constantly,” he replied. “The accounts are inaccurate. Seven blows and nine blows make sixteen; but the hammer was found to bear eighteen stains.”

There was no reasoning with him. Reason itself had become diseased.

I visited him for the last time in June. He was sitting on the floor amid thousands of white beans, sorting them into little heaps. The curtains were drawn against the distraction of daylight. His face had grown puffy and vacant; his bright eyes moved mechanically from heap to heap. He did not rise.

“What are you doing, Emberlin?”

“Approaching certainty.”

“About what?”

“The beans.”

He placed another bean upon a heap and whispered, “Four hundred and nine.”

I remembered the man who had once transformed an evening into a crystal Eden; who could touch the dullest fact and make it flower into paradox, history and laughter. That thaumaturge had vanished. In his place crouched this dreary animal, occupied by an operation which a child could perform, an idiot repeat, and a machine surpass.

On the wall above him he had written, in large black characters:

**EUPOMPUS GAVE SPLENDOUR TO ART BY NUMBERS.**

I left without saying good-bye.

It is customary to pity such obsessions as maladies, and no doubt pity is proper when one considers the sufferer’s helplessness. Yet I confess that my pity for Emberlin was mingled with a disgust so violent that even now I cannot wholly excuse it. To see a rich mind impoverish itself is worse than to see a miser starving beside gold; for the miser at least preserves the treasure, whereas the fanatic melts it down to manufacture his chains.

I have since reconsidered the death of Eupompus. Emberlin had said he killed his disciples and himself because he was mad. I rather believe the contrary.

For years Eupompus had been mad peacefully, industriously and with the approval of his school. Madness painted the swans, planted the quincunxes, marshalled the constellated citizens and assembled the ninety-nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine Cyclopes. Madness built systems, founded a terminology, attracted commentators and called itself Pure Number. It was patient, logical and complacent.

But perhaps, on that final morning, as he stood beneath the unfinished Totality with the hammer in his hand, sanity returned.

Perhaps he saw—not gradually, but in one intolerable flash—the fourteen wasted years, the rotting canvases, the beans, the tiles, the solemn disciples counting their breaths; saw Art reduced to inventory, God to a cipher, the universe to a ledger, and his own magnificent intelligence gnawing numbers like a rat gnawing bones. Perhaps Ptolemon and Bion approached him chanting the sacred progression. Perhaps their faces expressed the serene idiocy of perfect converts.

Then he struck them.

And, having destroyed what he could of Eupompianism, he climbed the dome and destroyed its author.

# The Cartographer of Lost Roads

On the morning the road disappeared, Mara Venn was painting a blue line across the northern wall of her workshop.

She had just reached the place where the highway crossed Bellwater Bridge when a sound like distant thunder rolled beneath the floorboards. The jars on her shelves trembled. A compass fell from its hook, struck the table, and spun so violently that its needle snapped.

Mara set down her brush.

Outside, the town of Orison was waking beneath a gray autumn sky. Shopkeepers lifted shutters. Chimneys breathed smoke. The clock in the courthouse tower announced seven with a tired bell.

Beyond the last houses, however, where the Royal Road had always run east between the wheat fields, there was now only grass.

Not broken stone. Not an unfinished track. Grass—green, wet with dew, and apparently ancient. It stretched unmarked from the town’s boundary to the hills.

By eight, half of Orison had gathered to stare.

“It was here last night,” said the baker.

“My brother drove his cart along it at sunset,” said a woman holding a basket of eggs.

Mayor Foss stood at the edge of the grass with his boots planted wide, as though he could intimidate the road into returning. “Someone has stolen the paving stones.”

“All twelve miles of them?” Mara asked.

The mayor frowned. He disliked questions that made his declarations seem foolish.

Mara knelt and pressed her fingers into the soil. The roots were thick and tangled. No stones lay beneath them. No scars marked the land. Yet she knew the road had existed. She had walked it as a child, traveled it as an apprentice, and drawn it on more maps than she could count.

She returned to her workshop, where the unfinished map covered an entire wall. Orison sat at its center, carefully rendered in black ink. Roads spread from it like veins: north to the salt coast, south through the vineyards, west toward the capital, and east across Bellwater Bridge.

But the eastern road was gone from the map.

The blue line she had been painting now ended at the town gate. Beyond it lay blank plaster.

Mara touched the empty space. The paint was dry.

Behind her, someone cleared his throat.

A boy stood in the doorway. He was perhaps twelve, narrow as a fence post, with a patched coat and dark hair falling into his eyes. Mara had seen him around town delivering messages for the postmaster.

“You’re the mapmaker,” he said.

“Cartographer.”

“That means mapmaker.”

“Yes.”

The boy entered without invitation and placed a small wooden box on her table. “My grandfather said to give you this if a road vanished.”

Mara stared at him. “Your grandfather expected this?”

“He expected everything. That was his worst habit.”

“What is your name?”

“Ivo Vale.”

Mara knew the name. Eli Vale had been Orison’s postmaster for forty years, until his death three days earlier. He had known every road, footpath, and gate in the province. People claimed he could address a letter to “the yellow house near the hill where the goats escaped” and have it delivered by noon.

Mara opened the box.

Inside lay a brass compass, a folded sheet of paper, and a small silver key. The compass had no letters marking its directions. Its needle pointed east, toward the blank wall.

The note was written in a shaking hand.

*Mara Venn,*

*If you are reading this, the Forgetting has begun.*

*Roads do not vanish because no one walks them. They vanish because no one remembers where they lead.*

*Follow the compass. Take the boy. Trust no map that changes while you sleep.*

*And whatever happens, do not let the road beneath the lake be forgotten.*

*Eli Vale*

Mara read it twice.

Then she looked at Ivo. “What lake?”

“I hoped you knew.”

At noon, the southern road disappeared.

A merchant caravan had just passed through the gate when the cobbles faded beneath the horses’ hooves. The animals panicked. One wagon overturned in what suddenly became a field of thistles.

Fear moved quickly through Orison. People rushed home and barred their doors, as if disappearance were a wolf that might enter through an open window. Mayor Foss ordered guards to watch the remaining roads. The guards obeyed, though no one could explain what they were meant to watch for.

Mara packed food, rope, chalk, two lanterns, and her father’s old surveying tools. She covered the wall map with canvas.

“You’re really taking me?” Ivo asked.

“No.”

“But the letter said—”

“Your grandfather was not in charge of me when he was alive, and death has not promoted him.”

Ivo folded his arms.

Mara locked the workshop and stepped into the lane. The compass needle swung toward the eastern gate.

Ivo followed.

She stopped. “Go home.”

“I live above the post office. Since Grandfather died, Mayor Foss says I’ll be sent to the city orphan house next week.”

Mara hesitated.

“I know the eastern road better than you,” he continued. “I delivered letters to every house between here and Bellwater.”

“There are no houses between here and Bellwater.”

His face changed. “There were yesterday.”

Mara turned toward the fields.

She remembered the road and the bridge. She remembered milestones mottled with lichen. But she could not recall a single house.

“Come,” she said.

They walked east across the grass.

The compass guided them where the road had been. At first, Mara could feel the memory of it beneath her feet: a gentle rise, a turn beside a stone wall, the long descent toward Bellwater. Yet the farther they went, the less certain she became. Landmarks dissolved inside her mind. Had there been an inn near the first milestone? A shrine beneath an oak? Whenever she reached for a memory, she found only fog.

Ivo remembered more.

“The Tern family lived there,” he said, pointing to an empty slope. “They had five daughters and a red dog.”

“How do you know?”

“I brought them letters.”

A little farther on, he stopped beside a stand of birches.

“There was a house here.”

Nothing remained but leaves and white trunks.

Ivo pushed into the grove. Mara heard him searching. Then silence.

She found him kneeling beside a shallow hollow, holding a blue glass marble.

“The youngest girl gave me this,” he said. “Her name was Sella.”

As soon as he spoke the name, the air shivered.

For an instant, a house stood among the trees.

It was small, with yellow curtains and smoke rising from its chimney. A red dog slept by the door. Somewhere inside, children laughed.

Then the vision vanished.

Ivo closed his fist around the marble.

“Names hold things,” Mara whispered.

The compass needle jerked onward.

By evening they reached the Bellwater gorge. The bridge was gone.

The river rushed fifty feet below, white against black rocks. On either side, the grassy banks ended at the cliff.

Mara unpacked her rope.

Ivo peered over the edge. “You can’t climb that.”

“I have climbed worse.”

“When?”

Mara looked down. She could not remember.

The forgetting was inside her now, quietly removing pieces.

She forced herself to speak aloud. “My name is Mara Venn. I am thirty-four years old. I learned cartography from Master Ansel in the capital. My father was Tomas Venn, a surveyor. My mother was Lysa, who sang while she cooked and cheated at cards.”

Ivo watched uneasily.

“Your turn,” she said.

“My name is Ivo Vale. I’m twelve. I hate boiled carrots. My grandfather snored. My mother was named—”

He stopped.

Mara waited.

His face went pale. “I don’t know.”

She took out her notebook and wrote everything they had said. Beneath it, she added: *Ivo’s mother had a name.*

They climbed down at sunset.

The rock was wet, but iron rings had been driven into the cliff where the bridge supports once stood. Proof, Mara thought. The world might forget, but iron resisted.

They crossed the river on a fallen pine and climbed the opposite side in darkness.

At the top stood an inn.

It appeared so suddenly that Mara nearly cried out. Warm light glowed in its windows. A painted sign swung above the door, showing a white stag beneath three stars.

“I remember this place,” she said.

“I don’t,” said Ivo.

Inside, a fire burned low. The innkeeper was an old woman with silver hair bound in a red scarf. She showed no surprise at seeing travelers arrive from a roadless night.

“You’re late,” she said.

“For supper?” Ivo asked.

“For the end of things.”

Her name was Nella. She served them onion soup and hard bread, then listened while Mara described Eli’s note.

At the mention of the road beneath the lake, Nella crossed herself.

“So the postmaster found it,” she said.

“Found what?” Mara asked.

“The first road.”

Nella locked the door, drew the curtains, and added wood to the fire.

“Long ago,” she began, “before the kingdom and the border stones, people traveled by a road that joined every place to every other place. Not through distance, but through memory. If you knew where you wished to go—and remembered why—you could find the way.”

“That sounds impossible,” Mara said.

“Most old truths do.”

According to Nella, kings had feared the first road because armies could not guard it and taxes could not control it. So they ordered it drowned beneath a man-made lake. New roads were built: straight, numbered, measured, and watched. In time, the first road became a legend.

“But forgotten things do not die,” Nella said. “They grow hungry.”

Ivo put down his spoon. “Why are the other roads disappearing?”

“Because the first road is taking back what was made from it. Every path carries a little of its memory. Now someone has opened the lock beneath the lake.”

Mara placed the silver key on the table.

Nella stared at it.

“Or someone means to,” she said.

That night Mara dreamed of roads.

They coiled beneath fields like roots. They slept under houses, crossed deserts, and ran along the bottom of the sea. Millions of footprints shimmered upon them: merchants, soldiers, pilgrims, fugitives, children. Every traveler left a memory behind.

At the center of them all lay a black lake.

Something beneath its water opened an eye.

Mara woke before dawn. The inn was cold.

Ivo was gone.

So were the compass and key.

She found a note weighted by the blue marble.

*I remembered my mother’s name. She is Ada Vale. Grandfather said she died when I was born, but last night I remembered letters from her. I delivered them without knowing. She lives beyond the lake.*

*I have to find her.*

Mara swore, packed quickly, and ran outside.

The inn had vanished.

Behind her stood only ruined foundations overgrown with moss.

Ahead, frost silvered a road.

It was narrow and broken, but it was real.

Mara followed.

Throughout the morning, the country shifted around her. Fields became forest, forest became bare hills, and once she crossed a village where every house stood open and empty. She kept speaking as she walked, naming what she knew.

“My name is Mara Venn. I am a cartographer. Ivo Vale is twelve. His mother is Ada. He hates boiled carrots.”

Sometimes she repeated facts from her notebook. Sometimes she added memories before they could be stolen.

“I broke my left wrist at nine. My father carried me six miles home. My mother’s favorite song was ‘The Lantern and the Lark.’ I once loved a woman named Celia Dorn, who left because I would not.”

The last memory hurt. That reassured her.

By afternoon, she reached Lake Orra.

It filled the valley from cliff to cliff, perfectly still beneath the white sky. No birds crossed it. No reeds moved along its shore. At the water’s edge, Ivo stood beside a tall man in a dark green coat.

The man held Eli’s compass. Ivo held the key.

“Mara!” the boy called. “This is the King’s cartographer.”

Mara approached slowly.

The tall man bowed. “Sabin Rook, Master of Royal Maps.”

Mara knew the name. Every official map in the kingdom bore his seal.

“You opened the first road,” she said.

“Not yet.” He smiled. “The lock requires someone who remembers both a lost road and a lost person. Young Ivo has been remarkably useful.”

Ivo stepped away from him.

“You said my mother was beneath the lake.”

“She may be.”

“May be?”

Rook sighed. “Memory is not a ledger, child. It contains errors.”

Mara saw confusion twist Ivo’s face.

“Why do this?” she asked.

Rook turned toward the lake. “The kingdom is collapsing. Provinces rebel. Borders close. Roads are blocked by armies and tollgates. But the first road can connect every city instantly. No hunger. No isolation. No war lasting longer than a day.”

“Or an army arriving anywhere in an hour.”

“Tools obey their users.”

“Tools change their users.”

Rook’s smile thinned. “You sound like Eli. He guarded this secret for decades while people suffered for lack of it.”

“He gave me the key.”

“He gave the key to a grieving boy who would lead it here.”

Ivo looked down at the silver object in his hand.

Mara understood then. Eli had not merely predicted events. He had arranged them.

“Where is the lock?” she asked.

Rook pointed.

Beneath the lake’s clear surface, stone steps descended into darkness. At their foot stood an iron gate.

The water should have hidden it, yet once Mara saw the gate, the whole drowned road became visible. It ran from the shore into the depths, pale as bone.

The compass needle pointed toward it.

Rook took off his boots and stepped into the lake. The water did not ripple. He walked downward, but it rose no higher than his ankles, as though the road carried its own world around it.

Ivo followed.

Mara seized his shoulder. “You don’t know what is behind that gate.”

“My mother.”

“You hope.”

He faced her, angry and frightened. “That’s more than I had yesterday.”

Rook called from below. “The Forgetting will continue. By tomorrow, Orison may have no roads. By next week, it may have no doors. In a month, people will forget that other places exist.”

“Is he telling the truth?” Ivo asked.

Mara looked at the road disappearing into darkness.

“Yes,” she said. “I think he is.”

They descended together.

The lake hung above them like a glass sky. Silver fish passed overhead. On both sides of the road stood drowned trees, their branches lifted as if in surrender.

At the gate, Rook pointed to a keyhole.

Words had been carved into the iron:

*NO ROAD OPENS WITHOUT A FARE.*

“What fare?” Ivo asked.

“A memory,” Rook said. “A true one.”

He reached for the key, but Ivo pulled back.

“My mother first.”

Rook’s expression hardened. “Open the gate.”

“No.”

The cartographer moved quickly. He struck Ivo and tore the key from his hand.

Mara lunged, but Rook shoved her against the gate. The back of her head hit iron. Light burst across her vision.

Rook inserted the key.

The gate spoke.

Its voice was the sound of footsteps in an empty station.

**WHAT WILL YOU GIVE?**

Rook answered without hesitation. “I give the memory of my home.”

The key turned.

For a moment, sadness crossed his face. Then it vanished.

“Where was I born?” he murmured.

The gate opened.

Darkness rushed out.

Not shadow, but absence. It poured around them, filled with whispering voices and half-remembered destinations. Mara heard the names of vanished towns. She saw streets erased by conquest, footpaths abandoned after plagues, stairways from demolished houses. The first road had gathered them all.

Rook laughed and stepped through.

The darkness swallowed him.

Then the road woke.

A tremor ran beneath Mara’s feet. Above, the lake cracked from shore to shore—not the water, but its reflection, splitting like a mirror. Through those cracks Mara glimpsed Orison. The courthouse tower faded. Houses drifted apart, each becoming lonely in an endless field.

The first road was not reconnecting the world. It was devouring every lesser path until only itself remained.

Ivo stood before the open gate, blood on his lip.

A figure appeared in the darkness beyond.

A woman.

She had Ivo’s dark hair and narrow face. She stretched out her hands.

“Ivo,” she called.

He took a step.

Mara caught him. “Wait.”

“That’s her.”

“Maybe.”

The woman smiled. “Little bird,” she said. “Come to me.”

Ivo began to cry.

Mara felt his body lean toward the gate.

Then he whispered, “She never called me that.”

The woman’s smile remained, but her face emptied.

Ivo stepped back.

The figure dissolved into the dark.

**THE ROAD IS OPEN,** said the gate.

“How do we close it?” Mara demanded.

**WHAT IS REMEMBERED MAY RETURN. WHAT IS GIVEN MAY BEAR THE WEIGHT.**

Mara understood the words in the way one understands a map after long study: not piece by piece, but all at once.

The roads had vanished because people remembered destinations but forgot journeys. They wanted arrival without distance, connection without effort, maps without stories. The first road had fed upon that neglect.

To close it, someone had to give not one memory, but enough to restore the roads it had consumed.

She opened her notebook.

“My name is Mara Venn,” she began.

The darkness stirred.

“I walked the eastern road when I was seven, holding my father’s hand. At the second milestone we ate pears. At Bellwater Bridge he lifted me so I could see the swallows nesting beneath the arch.”

A golden line appeared under her feet, running back through the drowned valley.

“I traveled south at nineteen to study in the capital. It rained for six days. At the Red Fox Inn, a woman named Celia kissed me beside the stable.”

Another line flared.

Mara continued. She named every journey she could remember. Roads in winter. Roads under summer dust. Roads taken in hope, anger, duty, and grief. With each memory, a path of light spread outward through the gate.

But the darkness took payment.

Her father’s face disappeared first.

Mara faltered. She knew she had loved him, yet could no longer picture his eyes.

“Mara,” Ivo said, “stop.”

She remembered the mayor’s orchard path, the cliff road to the sea, the alley behind her childhood home.

Her mother’s song vanished.

She remembered crossing the capital at dawn.

The name Celia became a blank space in her heart.

Golden roads multiplied until the darkness began to fracture. Through the cracks came daylight, birdsong, the creak of wagon wheels.

Still the gate remained open.

“I don’t have enough,” Mara whispered.

Ivo took her hand.

“My name is Ivo Vale,” he said. “I delivered a letter to Sella Tern on the eastern road. She gave me a blue marble.”

A line of light ran toward the birch grove.

“I carried medicine to the miller during the snowstorm. I walked the north road with Grandfather. He complained about his knees every mile.”

The gate groaned.

Ivo’s memories joined Mara’s, small roads and ordinary errands, each as bright as a king’s highway.

“I remember my mother’s name,” he said.

Mara tightened her grip. “You don’t have to give that.”

“Yes,” he said. “I do.”

He faced the darkness.

“Her name was Ada Vale. She wrote twelve letters to my grandfather asking to see me. He hid them because she was ill and he was afraid. I found them after he died. She lived in a village called Lorn, beyond the lake.”

The light became blinding.

“I remember her,” Ivo said, sobbing. “And I give the road her name.”

The gate slammed shut.

The lake fell.

Water struck them with the force of a collapsing wall. Mara felt herself thrown upward, tumbling through cold and silver bubbles.

Then she was lying on the shore, coughing.

Ivo lay nearby, still breathing. In his hand was the brass compass. Its needle pointed west, toward home.

Across the lake, roads reappeared.

They came first as pale lines in the grass, then as dirt tracks, then cobbles and bridges and wheel-worn stone. Birds rose from trees. Far away, bells rang from villages the world had nearly lost.

Mara tried to remember why they had come.

There had been a gate, a man in green, a woman’s name.

She found only fragments.

Ivo sat up.

“Do you know me?” she asked.

He looked at her for a long moment. “You’re the mapmaker.”

“Cartographer.”

“That means mapmaker.”

She laughed, though she did not know why the words made her want to cry.

They returned to Orison two days later.

The eastern road lay beneath their feet, solid and familiar. The Tern family’s house stood among the birches, and a red dog barked at them from the door. Bellwater Bridge arched above the river. Every milestone had returned.

Yet some things remained lost.

Mara remembered her parents’ names but not their faces. She knew she had once loved someone in the capital, though she could not recall whom. Ivo remembered that he had searched for his mother, but her name was gone.

In spring, Mara painted a new map on the northern wall of her workshop.

It showed the kingdom’s highways, village lanes, forest trails, and forgotten paths. Beside every road, she wrote not only where it led, but who had traveled it and why.

*Here Tomas Venn carried his injured daughter home.*

*Here a boy delivered medicine through snow.*

*Here two travelers crossed a river after the bridge was forgotten.*

People came from distant towns to add their journeys. They brought stories of pilgrimages, escapes, homecomings, and wrong turns that became fortunate. Ivo recorded each one in careful handwriting.

Years later, travelers said Mara’s map was the most accurate in the kingdom, though it contained roads no surveyor could find and omitted several that appeared on royal charts.

When asked how a map could be accurate if it did not show the world exactly as it was, Mara would smile.

“A road is not only the ground beneath your feet,” she would say. “It is also the reason you chose to walk.”

And on quiet evenings, when the lamps were lit and rain whispered against the windows, the brass compass sometimes trembled on its hook.

Its needle would turn toward the eastern wall, where Mara had painted a black lake and, beneath it, a gate without a key.

Then Ivo would open the great book of journeys and read aloud.

The compass would grow still.

And every road in the kingdom would remember its way home.
